Large-context cache safety

Shared cache-reuse safety stops for large contexts across every Gateway provider and client.

About 9 min read · 2 sections

On this page
01 Chat overflow trimming 02 Recovery verification

Every inference request through Gateway's Responses and Messages APIs passes the same cache guard. This includes Codex, Claude, Copilot, Grok, local models and OpenRouter or other API providers. Desktop, CLI, mobile and other clients using those APIs receive the same protection on every supported host OS. WebSocket inference upgrades remain unsupported and are refused before provider execution. SDK control WebSockets do not bypass the downstream inference guard. The separate Claude Desktop native auxiliary classifier also uses this guard, with its own account/model budget. Its runner reports count-only cache usage before a later stream failure as well as on success. Missing cache fields remain unknown; the helper cannot reset the ordinary chat budget or opt into its compaction recovery budget.

A provider declared selfHosted: true is measured but never stopped. It records outcome: observed where another provider would record blocked, and the request runs. A cache miss on a model you run yourself costs prefill time, not quota or credit, and stopping the worker only moved its task onto a metered fallback. Qwen lost ten worker turns this way between 1 and 3 November 2026. Gateway requires a loopback or tailnet inference provider for this setting but never infers it, because a local address can be a proxy to a metered upstream. Leave it off for anything that forwards.

During active work, a request with at least 65,536 uncached input tokens and more uncached than cached tokens counts as a large cache miss. After two consecutive measured misses, Gateway allows one more caller request to establish reuse. If that request is also cold, the fourth request stops before provider execution. This tolerates a temporary provider cache loss without an unlimited resend loop. Cache expiry or routing changes can happen upstream during active work; a cache miss does not establish that the person caused it. A read covering at least 75% of the preceding cached prefix is treated as reuse, so genuinely large new tool results do not cause a false rewrite alarm. A miss streak containing unreported cache usage or a provider refusal keeps the two-miss limit. Unknown cache usage has a distinct explanation and is never presented as a measured zero.

A provider can raise the measured-miss allowance with cacheMissLimit (an integer from 3 to 12; default 3). The last allowed request is still reserved against parallel requests, and the cooldown and single recovery probe are unchanged. Use it only for a cheap metered provider whose prefix cache builds asynchronously: on 10 November 2026 a new DeepSeek Flash worker on OpenRouter was paused after three cold requests at about 7% cache reuse. Unknown cache usage and provider refusals keep the two-miss limit.

Before a safety stop, five minutes without request activity starts a fresh warm-up period. An idle chat can legitimately lose its provider cache or live session, so a cold seed after that gap does not combine with an old miss to block its first continuation. Admitted request attempts and completions refresh activity. A per-conversation in-flight count prevents overlapping long requests from expiring each other's history; it is released even on error or cancellation. A long-running inference is therefore not mistaken for idle time. Once the miss limit is reached, a fixed five-minute cooldown starts. Blocked retries do not move its deadline. After it expires, Gateway allows one recovery probe on the next caller request. Another large miss starts another cooldown; expiry does not grant a full three-request warm-up. There is no background inference or automatic replay. A probe that fails without reporting usage also uses its one admission and starts another cooldown. Actual cache reads still clear the consecutive-miss count. Intermittent misses separated by successful reuse do not constitute continuous uncached processing under this policy.

A follow-up sent during a turn cancels that request, and that says nothing about whether the cache works. It can also end the live session, as when Claude was writing a tool call, so the next request has to rebuild the chat. Gateway therefore does not count a request the caller cancelled before it finished, and it excuses the one rebuild after that cancellation. On 5 November 2026 two follow-ups in a row counted as two misses, and Gateway stopped a request that would have continued the rebuilt session cheaply. Only a caller's own cancellation qualifies: a timeout or shutdown still counts, and a client that disconnects after a finished response cancelled nothing. A chat can excuse four rebuilds this way; a real cache read of at least 65,536 tokens or an idle reset before a safety stop restores that allowance. After four, ordinary counting resumes, so a client that disconnects and retries in a loop still reaches the stop. The stop can therefore only follow a follow-up if more than four rebuilds in a row were cancelled or excused with no cache reuse between them.

A rebuild that the caller caused by changing its tools, instructions, thinking or Fast setting is excused in the same way during ordinary work. A cold recovery probe after a cooldown still starts another cooldown, even when its miss is excused. The provider reports client changes (for Claude, a fingerprint_changed reseed), and the next request continues the rebuilt session. On 8 November 2026 a resumed chat of about 600,000 tokens seeded cold, Codex then added 39 MCP tools 17 seconds later, and Gateway stopped the warm request that followed. These rebuilds use the same four-rebuild allowance, so a tool list that changes on every request still reaches the stop. A compaction window change or idle expiry is not a client change and still counts.

The idle-aware policy's one-time adoption grants inactive inherited histories a fresh bounded warm-up, including old entries without trustworthy timestamps. In-flight conversations retain their history. A process-wide adoption marker prevents later module reloads from repeatedly clearing a safety stop. A late legacy write after that handoff stays conservative until real idle is observed. Provider, model and caller identity remain the scope. No new user turn, reconnect or provider reseed alone resets the guard; only the cancellation and client-change rules above excuse a rebuild.

A provider refusal also ends the live session, so the next message rebuilds the chat. The refused request always counts as a miss when it was cold, and a refused request that reports no usage counts as one of unknown cache reuse if its input is at least 262,144 bytes, about 65,536 tokens. Repeated refusals therefore stop after two resends. A rebuild that follows a refusal gets the same single pass as one after a cancellation, so a chat that recovers is not stopped on its warm next message. That pass sits outside the four-rebuild allowance, because the refusal itself counted and a refuse-and-rebuild loop therefore still reaches the stop. A refusal is never excused, even when the caller also cancelled it.

A cache failure receives a final HTTP 400 or terminal stream error telling the person how many seconds remain before another recovery attempt. It explains that the history is preserved and retries do not extend the cooldown. It never reports context_length_exceeded, marks a client's context full, or instructs automatic compaction. Real provider context overflows retain their normal context-limit code. Unchanged reconnects cannot repeat costly inference. Legacy x-harness-cache-recovery: 1 headers remain accepted for compatibility but do not authorize compaction or bypass the budget.

Claude's default live policy avoids a redundant one-shot warmup for identified histories whose serialized conversation is at least 256 KiB: it seeds the live CLI directly, so the next request can append to that same native history. This is a transport-size heuristic, not a tokenizer or context-window limit. Explicit claudeSessions.warmup choices remain authoritative. Small requests, standalone compaction/prewarm/memory requests, replay mode, capacity checks and preserved- session refusals retain their existing behavior. This optimization adds no standalone warmup or hidden inference retry.

The guard is scoped to the provider binding, model and stable caller thread or session. Anonymous requests share their binding/model budget. Count-only state survives client reconnects and in-place upgrades. It retains at most 4,096 recent entries; a full inference-process restart or eviction resets that history. Already-running concurrent requests cannot be recalled. This is a per-caller safety stop, not an account-wide spending ceiling.

The client can recover with conversation input at most half the byte size of the failed input; fixed top-level tools, instructions and metadata do not count toward that comparison. Compaction requests have a separate budget so they remain available for recovery, while repeated cold compactions also stop. Instructions inside the conversation retain their roles and count as conversation input.

The guard records each request's usage once. Providers can supply an internal, count-only observation before a terminal error: Claude CLI message-start usage, Anthropic message-start usage, Chat Completions usage chunks and Responses terminal usage are observed before later validation can fail. Copilot and other adapters' running usage events also feed the guard. Missing measurements do not erase a prior failure; input never reported by a provider cannot be measured.

context_cache_guard records only a hashed key, mode, fixed reason and count. It appears in recent diagnostics. Request bodies, instructions, tools and credentials are never saved by the guard.

Direct Claude/Codex subscriptions or other clients that bypass Gateway are outside this enforcement boundary. No native application or external runtime is patched by this feature.

Chat overflow trimming

vLLM rejects an oversized prompt with a plain 400. Gateway maps every such rejection, including "max_tokens must be at least 1, got 0" for a prompt that fills the window, to context_length_exceeded, so the client compacts or trims. A worker forked with far more history than the window allows can still trim one item per request for a long time; on 10 November 2026 three forked Qwen workers sent about 4,000 refused requests in 89 minutes. After 25 consecutive overflows for one conversation within ten minutes, Gateway refuses the next request locally with a non-retryable invalid_request that asks for a fresh worker with a compact handoff (fork_turns="none"). No provider call occurs. A completed request resets the count; it never changes caller history.

Recovery verification

Run node scripts/e2e-cache-recovery.mjs --package INSTALLED_PACKAGE --code CHECKOUT --root TASK_DIRECTORY after building the checkout. The isolated real SDK must allow three measured cold calls and stop the fourth without reporting context exhaustion. An unchanged retry must remain blocked without automatic compaction or another provider call. A separate explicit caller compaction command may then compact once and continue with smaller input in the same chat and model. The fixture uses synthetic inference and no account. --sdk ABSOLUTE_CANDIDATE qualifies a newly built Gateway SDK before packaging. The existing Gateway-only SDK accounting fix remains available for genuine context overflows. Cache safety no longer invokes that context-full marker.
